opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this goes back to a document I wrote around 2017, before GPT-1, even before a lot of the scaling-law work was formalized. The basic intuition was that all the cleverness people were putting into specific methods and architectures mattered a lot less than everyone thought. What really mattered was a fairly short list of things.

The first is just raw compute: how much you have. The second is the quantity of data. The third is the quality and distribution of that data. It needs to be broad enough to cover a wide range of what you want the model to be able to do. The fourth is how long you train. The fifth is an objective function that can actually scale. Pre-training on next-token prediction is one example, and I'd argue that RL objectives, done right, are another. Then there's a set of things that are almost more like plumbing: normalization, conditioning, whatever keeps the numerics stable so that the big blob of compute flows smoothly rather than hitting obstacles.

So that's roughly the list. The striking thing, at least to me, is how well that view has held up. People kept coming up with reasons it would stop working. The models can't reason, they can't do novel things, we'll run out of data. Each time the blob just kept going. Some of the specific techniques matter at the margin, and they matter a lot for efficiency, but the core thing is that you build a big blob of compute, you feed it the right data with an objective that scales, and you keep things numerically stable. Capabilities then come out in a surprisingly smooth and predictable way.

I'd add that I think the same hypothesis applies to RL now, not just pre-training. We're seeing the same kind of log-linear improvement as you scale up RL across a wide range of tasks. So I don't think of it as "pre-training scaling" versus "something new." It's the same blob, just applied in more places.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify the hypothesis as the same thesis as Rich Sutton’s “The Bitter Lesson.”

r003.rationale: It says cleverness in specific methods and architectures mattered less than people thought, while techniques mainly matter at the margin or for efficiency.

r004.rationale: It calls for data broad enough to cover a wide range of what the model should do.

r005.rationale: It identifies an objective function that can scale as a core ingredient, giving next-token prediction and RL objectives as examples.

r006.rationale: It says normalization and conditioning keep numerics stable so large compute can flow smoothly.

fable-5.1.text:
So the Big Blob of Compute Hypothesis is something I wrote down around 2017, and the core claim is actually pretty simple, maybe even a little deflationary. The claim is that there's a small number of ingredients, and if you have those ingredients and you scale them together, you get intelligence. You don't need some brilliant new idea every six months. You just need to keep turning the crank.

The first ingredient is raw compute. Just the number of floating point operations you can throw at the problem. This is the one people focused on the most, and the scaling laws showed that if you increase compute by some factor, the loss goes down in this smooth, predictable, almost boringly reliable way.

The second is data. You need a lot of it, and it needs to be at least somewhat diverse. Early on the internet was basically free data lying on the ground, and now the question has become more about how you generate or synthesize data, how you use environments, how you get signal from the models themselves.

The third is the objective function. For a long time that was next-token prediction, and the remarkable thing is how far that alone takes you. Then reinforcement learning on top of it, whether from human feedback or from verifiable rewards, gives you a second axis to scale.

And then there's a fourth ingredient that people tend to underrate, which is that the architecture has to be scalable. The transformer wasn't magic, but it was something where when you made it bigger, it kept getting better instead of saturating. A lot of ideas from the 2000s and early 2010s would have worked fine if we'd just had the compute, and a lot of clever ideas that looked great at small scale washed out when you scaled up.

So the hypothesis is really a claim about where the leverage is. The leverage is not in cleverness per se. It's in finding the handful of things that scale, and then being willing to bet, with a lot of money and a lot of conviction, that they'll keep scaling before you have proof that they will. That's what made it feel like a hypothesis rather than an observation, because at the time most of the field thought we were going to hit a wall, and we just kept not hitting it.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that a relatively small number of things explain most of the progress. You need compute, you need data, and you need a way to train a sufficiently large model on that data. Then you need an objective that actually pushes the model to learn something useful, and a training process that’s stable enough to work at scale.

The hypothesis is that those things matter much more than a lot of the cleverness we tend to focus on. You can spend a long time designing a special architecture to give a model some particular capability. But often, if you take a fairly general architecture and give it more compute and more data, it develops that capability anyway—and a bunch of other capabilities you weren’t explicitly trying to build.

That doesn’t mean algorithms don’t matter. An algorithmic improvement that lets you get the same result with ten times less compute is enormously valuable. But the picture is less that we have to invent a separate mechanism for reasoning, for language, for coding, and more that there’s this common underlying process that gets better as you scale it.

The surprising part is how far that goes. You might expect scaling to improve prediction in a narrow sense. What you actually see is that improving prediction requires the model to learn increasingly sophisticated structure in the world.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that a lot of the progress comes from a relatively small number of ingredients: how much compute you have, how much data you have, the quality and diversity of that data, and your ability to train a large model stably. Then there are architectural and algorithmic improvements, but the hypothesis is that the precise details matter less than people often think.

If you get those ingredients right, you can take a fairly simple approach and scale it, and a surprisingly broad range of capabilities emerge. You don’t have to build a separate mechanism for reasoning, another for coding, and another for understanding language. A lot of those things come together in this big blob of compute.

That doesn’t mean you can just buy GPUs and everything happens automatically. There’s a lot of engineering and experimentation involved in making the whole thing work. But the underlying bet is that scaling a general learning process carries you much further than carefully hand-designing each capability.

r005.rationale: It does not state that progress requires an objective function that can continue to scale.

r006.rationale: It calls for training a large model stably, but does not identify numerical stability as necessary for effectively using large amounts of compute.
